title: Some Voters Are Asking AI Chatbots for Help With Their Ballots
summary:
Voting in the 2026 midterm elections has already started in the United States, and some voters are trying something new to get ready. They are asking AI chatbots to help them research the candidates and races on their ballots, NPR reports.

In Morgantown, West Virginia, Adam Johnson, 40, spent hours one September evening going over his ballot with ChatGPT, a chatbot made by the company OpenAI. He asked it to list every race on his ballot and then to compare candidates based on the values he cares about. Johnson said the chatbot is "kind of a people pleaser" that tends to speak positively about whatever he leans toward.

Other voters told NPR they use chatbots to learn about smaller local races that get little news coverage, to make tables comparing candidates, and to check whether claims they see online are true. Lisa Veldran, 65, of Madison, Wisconsin, used Google's Gemini chatbot to compare two candidates for governor. She said it can be a research tool, but people should remember who pays to build these bots and why. In Pennsylvania, author Lakshmi Iyer used the chatbot Claude to build a volunteer website that helps voters look up who is on their ballot.

Experts urge caution. Rafael Batista, a fellow at Johns Hopkins University who studies how AI shapes people's experiences, said chatbots may pick information that pushes users further toward what they already believe. Because AI companies do not explain how their models choose sources, he said, it is hard to know what biases they carry. OpenAI said it monitors its models to keep answers politically neutral.

Chatbots can also "hallucinate," which means giving false or made-up answers. Batista suggested that voters keep their personal preferences hidden when they ask questions.
why_it_matters: As AI tools become part of how people learn about elections, understanding their strengths and weaknesses helps voters make informed choices.
